entities_and_workflows: Lift-out booking: the owner rings (or emails, or catches the marina manager on the pontoon); the office administrator puts a line in the book's lift-out tab with boat, owner, length, date and the work wanted

Hoist scheduling: each Friday the marina manager prints the next week from the book onto the hoist whiteboard, one column a day, and fits the boats into the tidal window (two hours either side of high water, two to six boats a day depending on the tide)
The daily sheet: printed off the whiteboard each morning for the yard crew, with boat, length, weight, berth, cradle tag number, owner's phone and a box for who drove
The lift: the hoist driver lifts, the yard foreman and crew chock and tie the boat into a numbered cradle on the hardstanding
Job card: written in triplicate off the book by the office administrator; top copy to the workshop wall, second to the office, third cable-tied to the boat
Workshop assignment: the workshop manager hangs the card on a hook and gives it to an engineer by proximity and skill (two engine specialists; GRP and antifoul to whoever has a roller)
Hours and parts: written on the card by the engineer, or reconstructed roughly on Friday; the workshop manager signs, the general manager signs anything over five hundred in parts
Invoicing: the signed card goes upstairs; the finance manager types it into the accounts package; in April six to eight weeks after launch
Launch booking: the launch date is taken when the boat comes out and written in the launches tab; changes arrive by phone in February and reach the book or the card but rarely both
Owner notification: nobody formally; the workshop manager rings the office or the owner; the owner usually rings first
Visitor lifts: twenty to thirty a year, same day, for surveys; no card, often no line in the book; they collide with booked slots

Insurance and lift records: the owner's insurance certificate is meant to be on file before a lift and a lift record (who drove, weight, date) after; both on the card, sometimes; inspected by the insurer in January; berthing itself stays in its own system, which the client says stays and is not moved (00:19:31, 00:35:50)

leanings.question: Does the hoist schedule hold one line a boat, or one row per movement?
leanings.option: One capacity-aware schedule across every hoist movement (lift-out, launch, relaunch, visitor lift, repeat lift), each a movement with its boat, type, date and tide window, checked against that day's tide-set capacity; whether that is a connected movements board or another arrangement is an implementation choice (FEEDBACK s18 item 1), provisional until a real build.

And one of the four on the board was a relaunch, not a lift, because a boat that came out in September for a quick job needed to go back in, and that was on Bernie's wall and not in the book at all.
in and out the same day, no card, and no line in the book half the time
So on a neap it's two boats. On a big spring it's five, six if Wojtek's on form.

leanings.question: Does the job card carry what work is done and what remains?
leanings.option: The card lists the requested work items, each marked done or remaining, updated by the workshop manager or the office; the printed sheet carries the remaining items; the launch warning fires on a launch inside the fortnight with work remaining, not on the date alone (FEEDBACK s18 item 2). A done mark is a person's claim that the work happened; the boat is the evidence (s22 line).
quotes: with the antifoul not done or the anodes not on or, in two cases, the engine in bits on the floor of the workshop
Boat name, owner, what they've asked for. Antifoul, anodes, engine service, whatever.
The antifoul's on, but the anode's in a box in the workshop.
Then the lads don't get logins in the first go. The office types, the lads read paper.
leanings.condition: who marks an item done and when (the workshop manager on her Friday round, or the office from the returned sheet), to be asked of the workshop manager on the fifth
leanings.pattern: a pain with no element that fixes it

leanings.question: Is the boat its own record, with movements and cards under it, or is the lift the boat?
leanings.option: A boat record (name, owner, length, weight, this season's cradle, insurance on file) as the parent of its hoist movements and its job cards, so the weight is typed once and a boat lifted twice is one boat with two movements.
quotes: So the weight is a fact about the boat that lives in three places or none.
Or none. Yes. Usually none.
We've got the weights for maybe two thirds of the regulars. In Maxine's head, mostly. Some on the sheet.
leanings.condition: whether the book has one line per boat per season or a boat list behind its two tabs, which only the office administrator can say (the twenty-eighth)

leanings.question: Does the workshop wall become a view of the cards by engineer?

leanings.question: How does a printed sheet show that it is out of date?
leanings.option: Every printed sheet and printed card carries the time it was printed and the schedule it came from; a booking taken after the print shows on the schedule as not yet on paper (a printed-at stamp on the day or the movement).

leanings.condition: whether the office prints once a morning or on demand, to be asked of the marina manager on the fifth and the office administrator on the twenty-eighth

leanings.question: What does 'insurance on file: yes' mean a year later?
leanings.option: The yes carries the date the certificate was seen and, where the certificate states one, its expiry; a yes older than the certificate's period shows as lapsed before the January inspection. The yes is the office's claim that a document is on file, never the document.
quotes: Before a boat comes out we're supposed to have the owner's insurance certificate on file, and after it comes out there's a lift record, who drove, what it weighed, date.
Not the certificate itself. Whether we've got it.
leanings.condition: whether certificates carry an expiry the office records, to be asked of the finance manager on the fifth
